title: Consecutive Characters
statement: Call the **power** of a string the length of its longest non-empty block of consecutive positions that all hold the same character. Given the string `s`, return its power.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every substring for a single repeated letter works but is slow. A block of equal letters is a maximal run, so one left-to-right pass can track how long the current run is and keep the longest seen.

## Approach

1. Start `best` and `run` at 1: the first character alone is a run of length 1.
2. For each index `i` from 1, compare `s[i]` with `s[i - 1]`.
3. If they match, the run grows by one; otherwise a new run of length 1 begins.
4. After each step, update `best` with `run`.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "leetcode"`. At `i = 1` (`e` after `l`) the run resets to 1. At `i = 2` (`e` after `e`) the run becomes 2 and `best = 2`. Every later character differs from the one before it, so `run` keeps resetting to 1 and `best` stays `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the string.
- Space: O(1): just two counters.

## Pitfalls

- Starting `best` at 0 breaks a one-character string, whose power is 1.
- Update `best` on every step, not only when the run ends, or a run at the very end of `s` is missed.
- Reset `run` to 1, not 0, because the new character already counts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `best` | longest run found so far |
| `run` | length of the run ending at index `i` |
| `i` | current index in `s` |

narration.2: Any non-empty string has a run of at least 1, so best starts there.
narration.3: The run ending at index 0 is just the first character.
narration.5: Visit each character after the first.
narration.6: Does this character continue the run of the one before it?
narration.7: Yes: the current run gets one longer.
narration.9: No: a fresh run of length 1 starts here.
narration.11: Keep the longest run seen so far.
narration.13: best now holds the power of the string.
